newsitem.title: JAPAN: Dollar trims gains vs yen by late Tokyo.
newsitem.headline: Dollar trims gains vs yen by late Tokyo.

text.p: 0632 GMT TRADED HIGH/LOW AS OF 0600 GMT

The dollar trimmed its gains against the yen by late Tokyo on Tuesday after having jumped in reaction to comments by Japanese Finance Ministry official Eisuke Sakakibara in morning trade, dealers said.
Although the dollar's downward bias has not been fully disregarded in the market, traders became reluctant to test its downside following Sakakibara's comments, they added.
Sakakibara, who has been appointed vice minister of international affairs at the ministry, told Reuters in a telephone interview: "The MOF's forex policy has not changed."
"As with the U.S. Treasury, (the ministry) does not have any intention at all of using foreign exchange rates as an instrument of trade policy," he added.
Traders rushed to cover their short positions following Sakakibara's comments, but gains were limited as Japanese investors were quick to sell the greenback for hedge purposes.
"Sakakibara's comments themselves were not very new, but he said it at the right time," one city bank dealer said.
Dollar short positions, which had been increasing amid lingering pessimism over the dollar's future outlook, have exaggerated the dollar's upward swing, dealers said.
Short-covering by interbank dealers boosted the dollar to 113.45 yen from around 112.50/60 yen immediately after Sakakibara's comments.

"I don't think the bullish trend towards the yen still exists, but the mood in the market has changed," a trust bank dealer said, adding traders who had been eager to test the dollar's downside are now taking a wait-and-see attitude ahead of Japan's current account surplus data due out on Wednesday.
Dealers said stronger-than-expected figures in the data could encourage traders to sell the greenback again but with a more careful attitude in the wake of Sakakibara's comments.

A Reuters poll of economists showed forecasts of a surplus ranging from 910 billion yen to 1.26 trillion yen, compared with a surplus of 355.7 billion yen in May 1996. The figures represent an increase ranging from 156 percent to 254 percent.

In the morning, comments by Finance Minister Hiroshi Mitsuzuka that he supports the view expressed by the Bank of Japan (BOJ) governor that the central bank will maintain its current monetary policy, also supported the dollar.

Meanwhile, Jiji news agency, quoting unnamed sources, reported on Tuesday that a high-ranking U.S. Federal Reserve Board official has stressed the need for Japan to maintain its low interest rate policy, partly to stabilise U.S. financial markets.

A foreign bank dealer said the market will keep focusing on trade issues, although Sakakibara said both the United States and Japan have no intention of using foreign exchange rates in their trade policy. Dealers also keeping close watch on possible comments from Japan-U.S. Business Council meeting in San Francisco, which started on Monday.
Dealers in Singapore said dollar/mark was seen on a steady upward path, supported by talk of more difficulties with European economic and monetary union on requirements for a single currency.
The dollar closed at 112.74/84 yen and 1.7530/40 marks in New York on Monday.
